<main class="s-page">

<header class="s-intro">
  <div>
    <p class="s-title" role="heading" aria-level="1">About</p>
    <p class="s-lede">I grew up near Lake Victoria in Homa Bay, western Kenya, where I learned to pay attention: to the weather, to the lake, to what people say and what they don't. That instinct has served me well in data work.</p>
  </div>
  <img class="s-intro__photo" src="../img/new profile pic.jpeg" alt="Portrait of Nichodemus Amollo">
</header>

<p>At KEMRI I managed oncology data, and it taught me something no methods course quite captures: data quality is a moral act. Every row is a person waiting for a diagnosis. That sense of responsibility has travelled with me into every job since.</p>

<p>Over eight years I have worked across the whole research lifecycle: designing digital survey tools for communities without internet, building the databases that receive the data, running high-frequency quality systems, leading field teams across three countries, and delivering reports and apps that programme teams actually use. Today I am a Data Analyst at <a href="https://gui2de.georgetown.edu/profiles/nichodemus-amollo/">Georgetown University's gui²de</a> in East Africa, where I build the data systems for studies including the Kenya HealthFin Diaries with FSD Kenya and the Re:BUiLD cash-plus targeting app for IRC.</p>

<p>I hold a BSc in Statistics from the University of Nairobi and am completing an MSc in Epidemiology and Biostatistics at JOOUST, where I also lecture part time. My research is on health financing and chronic care in Kenya; you can read it on the <a href="../research/publications.html">research page</a>.</p>

<p>What makes me useful is that I can work at both ends. I can sit with a community health worker and explain why data completeness matters, then walk into a boardroom, or ship a caseworker tool, so that findings and models become decisions.</p>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="gpak-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="gpak-h">GPAK Girls</h2>
  <p>In 2018, while serving as a volunteer local missionary with CGEC, I travelled from homestead to homestead in western Kenya and kept meeting girls whose problems the policies on paper had supposedly solved. I started paying for what I could out of my own earnings. That became <a href="https://www.gpakgirls.org/team">Girl Pride Africa Kenya (GPAK Girls)</a>.</p>
  <p>From 2018 to 2020 it ran largely on personal contributions while we built the structure needed to operate legally. LARCOD became our first partner organisation, and GPAK Girls was registered with the NGOs Co-ordination Board of Kenya in April 2020. Based in Homa Bay, it supports adolescent mothers and pregnant girls through psychosocial and mental health support, health referrals, education, livelihoods and family strengthening.</p>
  <p>A Director and programme team now run the organisation day to day. I contribute part time on data, technology, monitoring and evaluation, leadership and fundraising.</p>
</section>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="highlights-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="highlights-h">A few highlights</h2>
  <ul class="s-list">
    <li>Built the end-to-end data system for a 300-household, twelve-month health financial diaries panel at gui²de, pairing automated high-frequency checks with an <a href="https://ra-leaderboard.streamlit.app/">RA performance leaderboard</a> and a live issues app so supervisors fixed field problems during collection rather than at cleaning.</li>
    <li>Delivered the production application layer for <a href="https://rebuild.shinyapps.io/rebuild-targeting/">Re:BUiLD cash-plus targeting</a>, turning gui²de causal forest models over 6,260 participants into a caseworker-facing recommender.</li>
    <li>Ran the KEMRI oncology data systems (REDCap registry design, quality control and survival analysis) behind the Kisumu cancer surveillance dashboard launched with county health leadership.</li>
    <li>Led distributed field teams across Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, holding quality standards through remote coordination during the COVID-19 pandemic.</li>
    <li>First-author paper in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26963-8"><em>BMC Public Health</em></a> (2026) on financing constraints and chronic care in rural Kisumu, plus three first-author preprints since.</li>
  </ul>
</section>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="values-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="values-h">What drives the work</h2>
  <p>I believe data has a side. It either serves the people it was collected from, or it serves the institutions that collected it. My goal is always the former.</p>
  <p>That shows up in how I approach M&amp;E: as a learning system, not a compliance checklist. It shows up in how I train enumerators: I want them to understand why a question is structured the way it is, not just how to tap the screen. And it shows up in how I write reports: I want to change a decision, not demonstrate that I can run a regression.</p>
</section>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="life-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="life-h">Outside work</h2>
  <p>I keep goats and tend a kitchen garden in Homa Bay. There is something honest about agriculture; it keeps development work grounded in reality. I also love football, running, hiking and long conversations over tea that go further than they were supposed to.</p>
